question: Why did 18th-century Japanese cities escape the sewage crisis of European ones?
answer: Because excrement had a price. Farmers bought city waste as fertiliser, paying in cash or vegetables, so collectors carted it out instead of dumping it. In Osaka the right to sell a building's faeces belonged to the landlord, while the tenants sold their own urine.
move: Give a waste a price and someone will come to collect it.
reference: Hanley, Urban Sanitation in Preindustrial Japan, Journal of Interdisciplinary History, 1987
